editor_spans.body: Read in order, the week's Ukraine statements show how much London's line depended on Washington. On 9 October the government's response to a US–Russia agreement never says what the agreement contained. It repeats 'for as long as it takes' and then turns to energy markets and the cost of living.

By 12 October the Prime Minister was welcoming President Trump's 'reciprocal energy ceasefire'. He did not present it mainly as a way to protect Ukraine. He presented it as the quickest way to get diesel back onto world markets. Fuel prices at home seem to matter as much as Kyiv's power grid in shaping the UK position.

Two days later, Downing Street said Russia had attacked civilians and energy infrastructure since Trump called for the ceasefire, and concluded that Russia 'had no interest in peace'. The ceasefire London had welcomed had already failed, and the response was to speed up deliveries.

The figures behind 'double down' are small. £10 million of the new £45 million missile package will be brought forward, against £1.6 billion already committed over four years. Ministers were asked to 'draw up' further packages rather than announce them. The new step is diplomatic: pushing the IMF and the Warsaw Security Forum to copy the UK's ban on shipping services for Russian LNG. That uses London's shipping and insurance industry as leverage, which costs the UK budget little.

The rail headquarters and the Scottish devolution offer share one source: Burnham's belief in regional power. At Derby, the government names the East Midlands Combined Authority and its elected mayor as delivery partners. In Lanarkshire, he offers Scotland, through No10 North, a new model of power for its regions. The mayoral combined authority looks like the template he wants to apply across the country.

The Scottish offer is not neutral, though. It accuses Holyrood of being among Europe's most centralised devolved administrations. It also proposes that the UK government work directly with Scottish regions through its own offices. Describing it as 'two governments, one goal' plays down the challenge to the Scottish Government's authority over Scotland's councils and cities. The First Minister has an obvious reason to read it as Westminster going around Holyrood.

The Derby headquarters is a promise for later. Building starts in early 2029's run-up, in 2027, and finishes in spring 2029. Until then, the visible results of public ownership are a fare freeze, extra seats and trains ordered from Alstom. The building will hold up to 450 staff, which accounts for the 'hundreds of jobs'.

The most telling figure is not about Derby. Under 7% of the railway's workforce is under 25. The 600 apprenticeships over four years are funded from a general youth employment budget. They are a modest response to an industry whose skilled workforce is ageing faster than it is being replaced. The new owner's biggest task may be staffing, not ownership.

The most important part of the Commons statement came late and was worded carefully. The Prime Minister wants a 'serious dialogue' on the long-term relationship with the EU after the 20 November summit, says 'the British public will be the boss', and promises 'care and complete transparency'. He is preparing the ground for a bigger question than the food, emissions-trading and youth-scheme deals on the table. He also makes success at the summit depend on being openly willing to have that wider discussion.
